extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York / the American public and voters (circa 1787); readers concerned with constitutional design and the preservation of the Union
extracted.subtask_description: Political-pamphlet-style arguments about the deficiencies of confederacies and the necessary powers and structures a national (federal) constitution must have to preserve the Union and prevent anarchy. Emphasizes direct national authority, enforcement mechanisms, and historical precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation must operate directly on individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: "It must carry its agency to the persons of the citizens. It must, in short, possess all the means, and have a right to resort to all the methods, of executing the powers with which it is intrusted, that are possessed and exercised by the government of the particular States."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal laws should not depend on intermediate state enactments to take effect. The national government must be empowered to act directly upon citizens so its measures cannot be defeated by state inaction or evasive procedures. This direct operation prevents subtle subversions of federal authority and ensures enforceability without relying on state legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: National authority should be manifested through the courts of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: "The majesty of the national authority must be manifested through the medium of the courts of justice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordinary magistrates and the judicial system to execute national resolutions. A national judiciary gives the federal government a lawful, visible mechanism to enforce its laws and to distinguish legal exercises of power from unconstitutional usurpations, relying on judges' declarations and the people's capacity to defend the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dependence on a large standing army for enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that if the national government lacked power to act on individuals it would need "a large army constantly at the disposal of the national government" which would either be impossible to maintain or would degenerate into "a military despotism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions so that ordinary law-enforcement and judicial mechanisms—not perpetual military coercion—are sufficient to implement federal decisions. Relying on a standing army to enforce civil administration is impracticable (insufficient resources) and dangerous (risk of military despotism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate non-compliance from direct active resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: "The plausibility of this objection will vanish the moment we advert to the essential difference between a mere NON-COMPLIANCE and a DIRECT and ACTIVE RESISTANCE."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When national measures require state cooperation, states can defeat them merely by not acting (non-compliance) or acting evasively. If laws operate immediately on citizens, obstruction by state legislatures would require overt, unconstitutional acts subject to judicial and popular remedy. Thus constitutional design should minimize modes for evasive non-compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local governments have superior influence over citizens by proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: "It will always be far more easy for the State governments to encroach upon the national authorities than for the national government to encroach upon the State authorities... the people of each State would be apt to feel a stronger bias towards their local governments than towards the government of the Union."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that state administrations, being nearer to the people's daily concerns, will naturally command greater popular influence. Constitutional arrangements must take into account this asymmetry (e.g., by granting effective federal mechanisms) so the national government is not consistently undermined by local influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration of criminal and civil justice is the principal source of popular attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is one transcendant advantage belonging to the province of the State governments... I mean the ordinary administration of criminal and civil justice. This, of all others, is the most powerful, most universal, and most attractive source of popular obedience and attachment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because local courts and justice administration are highly visible and touch citizens' lives daily, states gain deep loyalty. Framers must consider how federal institutions can win public regard despite this advantage of state governments—e.g., by having federal laws and courts that operate visibly and fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confederacies historically tend toward anarchy or domination by powerful members
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical observations (Amphictyonic council, Lycians, Achaeans, Greek confederacies, Germanic body, feudal baronies) illustrating that confederacies often ended in internal disorder, domination by the strongest, foreign intervention, or dissolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical precedent to evaluate institutional designs: loose confederacies in practice have proved weak—either tyrannized by powerful members or dissolved into anarchy. This supports creating a closer national union with effective centralized powers to preserve the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller members are vulnerable to corruption or coercion by powerful members
rubrics_metrics.description: "The deputies of the strongest cities awed and corrupted those of the weaker; and that judgment went in favor of the most powerful party."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design safeguards against domination by large or influential states (or members). Historical examples show deputies or representatives from small states could be bribed or intimidated; constitutional mechanisms should reduce opportunities for undue influence and ensure equitable operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confederacies invite foreign intrigue and intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: When domestic associates cannot be found, recourse would be had to foreign powers, "who would seldom be disinclined to encouraging the dissensions of a Confederacy, from the firm union of which they had so much to fear." Examples: Philip of Macedon, Roman intervention in Greek leagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A weak confederacy creates openings for foreign powers to manipulate internal divisions. A national constitution should limit incentives and opportunities for external powers to exploit domestic discord by providing stronger internal unity and independent national capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambitious large members may seek to escape external control
rubrics_metrics.description: Delinquencies of the larger members might proceed from "an ambitious premeditation in their rulers, with a view to getting rid of all external control upon their designs of personal aggrandizement; the better to effect which it is presumable they would tamper beforehand with leading individuals in the adjacent States."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that powerful constituent states may pursue schemes to evade central constraints and recruit allies. Constitutional arrangements should limit opportunities for such behavior and provide mechanisms to check ambitious aggrandizement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguities in enforcement (e.g., financial contributions) open field for faction and oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: In the article of pecuniary contribution... "it would often be impossible to decide whether it had proceeded from disinclination or inability... The pretense of the latter would always be at hand... this problem alone... would open a wide field for the exercise of factious views, of partiality, and of oppression, in the majority that happened to prevail in the national council."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid institutional designs that allow easy pretense or ambiguity (such as inability vs unwillingness) in fulfilling federal obligations. Clear, directly enforceable provisions reduce opportunities for factional exploitation and unfair majoritarian oppression.
